title: Applying for a job: the letter, the CV and the interview
title_target: Jag ser fram emot att berätta mer vid en intervju.
goal: Write a Swedish cover letter and CV, answer the classic interview questions with confidence, and pull together everything you have learned in Svenska 103.
bekal: you can write a personal letter that shows rather than tells, at a *lagom* level of confidence
you can set out a Swedish CV and describe your languages and experience
you can answer and ask the standard questions in a job interview
wave: Go back to Unit 1 (Three layers of the past): retell Dian's six months in Göteborg in ten sentences, using the preteritum, the perfekt and the pluskvamperfekt at least twice each (*Hon flyttade…*, *Hon har lärt sig…*, *Innan hon kom hade hon…*).

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Det personliga brevet
dialogs.intro: A Saturday morning at a café in Haga. Dian's internship ends in a month, and a design consultancy in Stockholm is looking for a junior UX designer. Oskar reads the first draft of her cover letter.

notes: **Ett personligt brev** — literally "a personal letter": the Swedish name for a cover letter, pronounced **peh-SHOON-lit brehv**. It is usually one page, it opens with *Hej* + the recruiter's name, and it explains why this job and why you, in that order.

**Sista ansökningsdag** — the application deadline, printed on every Swedish job ad. Many employers interview candidates as applications come in (*löpande urval*, rolling selection), so the post may be filled before that date. Apply early.

**Visa det i stället** — the best advice for any Swedish application: don't claim qualities, prove them. A list of adjectives (*ambitiös, kreativ, flexibel*) reads as empty; one concrete example convinces. This is *lagom* applied to writing.

**Har lett** — *leda* (to lead) has the forms *leda, ledde, lett*, with the same short-vowel pattern as *föda, födde, fött* (to give birth). Revisit the irregular verbs from Unit 2 before you write about your experience.

**Så nöjd att…** — *så* + adjective + *att* expresses a result, exactly like English "so happy that…": *Hon var så trött att hon somnade på bussen.* **Hålla sig till fakta** (to stick to the facts) is reflexive: *Håll dig till ämnet!* (Stick to the subject!)

**Jag ser fram emot att…** — *se fram emot* (to look forward to) is a particle verb with the stress on *FRAM*: **seh FRAHM eh-MOOT**. Like the fixed prepositions in Unit 16, it is followed by **att** + the base form where English uses *-ing*: *att berätta*, *att höra från er*.

grammars.title: The personal letter: building blocks
body: A Swedish cover letter has a predictable shape. Use these blocks as a scaffold and fill them with your own examples. Address the company as **ni / er**: here *ni* is simply plural (all of you at the company), not the old polite form.

head: Part
Svenska
English
rows: Jag söker tjänsten som junior UX-designer, som jag såg på er webbplats.
I am applying for the position of junior UX designer, which I saw on your website.
Det som lockar mig med er är…
What attracts me to you is…
Under min praktik på … har jag…
During my internship at … I have…
Som person är jag nyfiken och lyhörd.
As a person, I am curious and a good listener.
Jag ser fram emot att berätta mer vid en intervju.
I look forward to telling you more at an interview.

after: **Lyhörd** (literally "keen of hearing") is a favorite word in Swedish job ads and letters: someone who listens and picks up on what others need. It is the perfect quality for a consensus culture.

grammars.title: Talking about your experience: the tenses together
body: A job application is a review of the whole verb system of Svenska 103. Each tense has its own job; mixing them correctly is what makes a letter sound fluent.

head: Use
Form
Example
rows: Jag studerade i Stockholm i två år.
När jag kom till Göteborg hade jag redan läst tre kurser i svenska.
Jag kommer att ta examen i juni.
Jag skulle gärna vilja jobba hos er.

after: The commonest mistake in applications is using the perfekt with a finished time: *Jag har studerat i Stockholm 2024* is wrong; with a fixed point in the past, use the preteritum: *Jag studerade i Stockholm 2024*.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Intervjun
dialogs.intro: Two weeks later, Dian has been invited to a video interview with the consultancy in Stockholm. She sits at the kitchen table in Majorna, with her notes just out of sight of the camera.

lines.text: Välkommen, Dian. Berätta lite om dig själv.

notes: **Berätta lite om dig själv** — the opening question of almost every Swedish interview. Aim for about a minute: who you are professionally, what you are doing now, and why you are here. *I grunden* (literally "in the ground") means "by training, basically": *Hon är sjuksköterska i grunden.*

**Det senaste halvåret** — "the past six months". With *det senaste* / *de senaste* Swedish needs no preposition: *de senaste två åren* (for the past two years). Note the perfekt: the internship is still going on.

**Just den här tjänsten** — *just* means "exactly, precisely", not English "only": *just nu* (right now), *just därför* (for exactly that reason). *En tjänst* (**shenst**) is a position, a post; it also means a favor: *Kan du göra mig en tjänst?*

**Berätta om en situation då…** — a competency-based question, very common in Swedish recruitment. Answer in three steps: the situation (*Vi skulle…*), what you did (*Jag lyssnade… och föreslog…*), and the result. Dian borrows the consensus language of Unit 18, which is exactly what a Swedish recruiter wants to hear.

**Så rädd … att jag hellre var tyst** — the strongest answer to the "weakness" question is a real weakness that you are already working on: *tidigare… nu…*. *Ta ordet* (literally "take the word") means to speak up, to take the floor.

**Det hörs inte** — *höras* (to be heard) is an *-s* verb: "it can't be heard", i.e. you would never know. The same verb gives *Vi hörs!* (Talk soon!) and *Vi hör av oss* (We'll be in touch). **Tack själv!** is the friendly reply to someone who thanks you: "Thank *you*!"

grammars.title: Nine classic interview questions
body: Swedish interviews are relaxed in tone but well prepared. Expect these questions, in roughly this order, and have the first sentence of each answer ready.

head: Question
What they want
A good start
rows: Jag är … i grunden och har…
Varför söker du den här tjänsten?
Mina kollegor brukar säga att jag…
Berätta om en gång då du…
Vi skulle… Jag… Resultatet blev att…
Var ser du dig själv om fem år?
Jag har tänkt mig runt … kronor i månaden.
Har du några frågor till oss?
Hur ser en vanlig arbetsdag ut?

after: *Mina kollegor brukar säga att jag…* (My colleagues usually say that I…) is the perfect *lagom* trick: you name a strength, but someone else says it for you.
Always have at least one question ready for the end. Having none can come across as a lack of interest.

blocks.text: A Swedish CV is short (one or two pages), factual and in reverse chronological order: the most recent job first. A photo is common but not required, and you never need to state your age, religion or marital status. The headings below are standard; keep them in this order.

head: Heading
English
What goes there
rows: three or four lines about who you are professionally

blocks.title: Dian's language section
items: **Indonesiska** — modersmål (native language)
**Engelska** — flytande (fluent)
**Svenska** — goda kunskaper, nivå B1 (good command, level B1)
Other useful levels: *mycket goda kunskaper* (very good command), *grundläggande kunskaper* (basic knowledge).

blocks.text: Under *Arbetslivserfarenhet*, describe each job with verbs in the preteritum (for finished jobs) and concrete results: *Ledde fyra workshops med kunder. Tog fram skisser till en bokningsapp.* Swedish CVs often drop the subject *jag* in these lines, just as English CVs drop "I".
You have reached the end of B1. Here is the whole level on one page. Read each example aloud; if one makes you hesitate, go back to that unit before you start Svenska 104.

blocks.title: Spiral review — the whole level
items: Write your own *personligt brev* for a job you would really like, in 150–200 words, using the building blocks from this unit.
Check it for the four B1 classics: BIFF in every subordinate clause, the right preposition after verbs and adjectives (Unit 16), preteritum with a finished time, and V2 after a fronted clause.
Then record yourself answering the nine interview questions, one minute each. Listen back: where you hesitate is where your next review should start.
